title: EDHEC Venture Capital — Final Exam 2025
notice: Derived study pack: questions are condensed and paraphrased from the 2025 EDHEC VC past paper; numerical answers and worked solutions are reproduced. IMPORTANT: the official file contains no marked MCQ answers, so the MCQ answer key in this pack is derived (inferred), not official — treat MCQ grading as practice only; the worked/numerical solutions are reproduced from the official file.

questions.prompt: VC firms typically use staged financing in order to:

choices.text: Incentivize the entrepreneur to exert effort and reach predefined milestones.
Acquire information about the founder's true ability, reducing asymmetric information.
Keep the option to abandon ventures with low early returns.
All of the above.

questions.solution: Staged financing does all three: it creates milestone incentives, reveals information about founder ability, and preserves the option to abandon weak ventures.

questions.prompt: Milestone-based contracting can create perverse incentives because:

choices.text: It lowers information asymmetry.
It reduces agency costs.
Entrepreneurs may distort effort to meet short-term measurable goals at the expense of long-term value.
Investors lose board control.

questions.solution: The contract rewards observable short-term milestones; the founder may game them instead of maximizing long-term value.

questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between seed-stage and Series A funding rounds?

choices.text: Series A investors typically require board seats; seed investors do not.
Seed-stage focuses on scaling operations; Series A focuses on product-market fit.
Seed-stage builds and validates the product; Series A scales the business.
Series A rounds require higher equity stakes from founders than seed rounds.

questions.solution: Seed money validates the product and early traction; Series A funds repeatable go-to-market and scaling.

questions.prompt: A cross-border VC chooses a common-law domicile primarily because:

choices.text: It lowers tax on carried interest.
It standardizes IFRS accounting.
Judicial precedent offers stronger enforcement of term-sheet rights and LP agreements.
It allows multiple carry classes.

questions.solution: Common-law jurisdictions rely on precedent, which investors see as more predictable and enforceable for complex contracts.

questions.prompt: A stock-options pool is 'fully diluted' when:

choices.text: Subsequent funding rounds fully dilute the ownership stake attached to the pool.
All options are exercised and converted into common shares.
Employees do not exercise their options because these have become worthless.
None of the above.

questions.solution: Fully diluted means every option, warrant and convertible security is treated as already converted into common shares.

questions.prompt: The key inputs of the venture-capital valuation model are:

choices.text: Investment, time-to-exit, exit value, hurdle rate.
Investment, time-to-exit, exit value, risk-free rate, risk premium.
Investment, number of rounds, exit value, hurdle rate.
Investment, number of rounds, exit value, risk-free rate, risk premium.

questions.solution: The VC method discounts the expected exit value at the hurdle rate over the time to exit, then solves for the required ownership.

questions.prompt: In venture capital, pre-money valuation is:

choices.text: Always higher than post-money valuation.
Always lower than post-money valuation.
Lower than post-money valuation if the venture makes progress after investment.
Lower than post-money valuation if the entrepreneur negotiates a good deal.

questions.solution: By definition, post-money = pre-money + investment, so pre-money is always lower (for a positive investment).

questions.prompt: Why might a VC prefer a lower valuation with stronger protective provisions to a higher valuation with weak protections?

choices.text: It increases the founder's control.
It balances risk and expected return more effectively.
It avoids dilution in future rounds.
It reduces capital-gains taxation.

questions.solution: A lower price improves the VC's return, while protective terms limit downside; together they improve the risk-return trade-off.

questions.prompt: In the VC method, which of the following would NOT affect the investor's required ownership?

choices.text: Expected exit value.
Time to exit.
Hurdle rate.
Liquidation preference.

questions.solution: Required ownership = I(1+h)^t / exit value. Liquidation preference changes the payoff split, not the ownership fraction.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of an anti-dilution clause in a term sheet?

choices.text: To prevent existing investor ownership from being diluted in future funding rounds.
To restrict the issuance of new shares to employees.
To limit the founders' ability to issue new equity.
To ensure debt obligations are paid before equity holders.

questions.solution: Anti-dilution adjusts the preferred conversion price in a down round, protecting the investor's effective ownership.

questions.prompt: Which clause aligns founder and investor incentives by allowing founders to 'earn back' shares through continued effort?

choices.text: Pay-to-play.
Reverse vesting.
Drag-along.
Convertible note.

questions.solution: Reverse vesting means founders already own the shares, but unvested shares can be repurchased if they leave; continued service earns them back.

questions.prompt: In a term sheet, pay-to-play provisions are designed to:

choices.text: Force existing investors to participate in later rounds to retain preferential rights.
Guarantee future investment opportunities to new investors.
Protect founders from dilution in future rounds.
Ensure anti-dilution adjustments always apply.

questions.solution: Pay-to-play converts non-participating preferred into common (or strips its preferences) if the investor does not fund its pro-rata share of a down round.

questions.prompt: When comparing U.S. and continental-European VC contracts, which is most accurate?

choices.text: European term sheets rely more on protective provisions.
U.S. deals emphasize relationship-based monitoring.
U.S. contracts are more legalistic; European deals rely more on trust and staged financing.
No difference once English law governs both.

questions.solution: U.S. venture contracts are typically longer and more rule-based; continental European deals often rely more on relationship governance and staging.

questions.prompt: A founder is terminated 'for cause' one year after a 4-year reverse-vesting agreement with a 12-month cliff. They held 4 million founder shares. How many shares remain theirs?

choices.text: 1 million.
3 million.
4 million.

questions.solution: The 12-month cliff vests 25% (1 million shares). The remaining 3 million are unvested and repurchased; the vested million stays with the founder.

questions.prompt: A VC invests in a convertible note with both a discount and a valuation cap. The dual benefits are:

choices.text: Only the cap applies in up rounds.
Only the discount applies in down rounds.
The VC captures upside if valuation soars and protection if it rises modestly.
It prevents conversion to equity.

questions.solution: The investor converts at the lower of the discounted price and the cap price: the cap gives upside in a hot round, the discount gives a cushion in a moderate round.

questions.prompt: Palooka Products is negotiating a VC term sheet to receive $5 million today. It expects an IPO in 5 years at an exit value of $50 million. The VC requires a 40% hurdle rate. What share of equity will the VC accept? (answer in %).
A startup has 5m founder shares. A VC invests $2m at an $8m post-money valuation and requires a 20% post-money option pool. Fill the cap table.

parts.prompt: How many shares are in the option pool (m)?
parts.solution: Investor fraction = 2/8 = 25%. Founders keep 100 - 25 - 20 = 55%. Total post-money shares = 5 / 0.55 = 9.0909m. Pool = 20% × 9.0909 = 1.8182m.

parts.prompt: How many shares does the VC receive (m)?
What percentage do the founders own after the round?

questions.prompt: Miller Venture Capital invested $5m in BST 8 years ago and received 1m convertible preferred shares (2 common shares each). After conversion BST has 15m shares; it will issue 3m new shares in the IPO.

parts.prompt: What fraction of BST's common shares will Miller own after the IPO? (in %)
parts.solution: Miller owns 1m × 2 = 2m common shares. Post-IPO shares = 15m + 3m = 18m. Ownership = 2/18 = 11.1%.

parts.prompt: If the stock trades at $25 after the first day, what is Miller's IRR? (in %)

questions.prompt: A startup plans four rounds and expects a $6bn strategic acquisition in 7 years. Round data (investment, years to exit, target multiple): Seed $1m / 7y / 8x; Series A $25m / 6y / 5x; Series B $50m / 4y / 4x; Series C $200m / 2y / 3x. Compute the fully diluted ownership at exit.

parts.solution: Work backwards along the target-multiple ladder. Series C post = exit / 3 = 6000/3 = 2000; C pre = 2000 - 200 = 1800. Series B post = 1800/4 = 450; B pre = 400. Series A post = 400/5 = 80; A pre = 55. Seed post = 55/8 = 6.875; Seed pre = 5.875. Seed ownership = 1/6.875 = 14.545%.

questions.prompt: Butchered Data (BD) raised $300k in convertible notes (20% discount, converts at the next round ≥ $2m). Two term sheets: Alpha invests $4m at a $9m post-money, 25% option pool, 1x non-participating liquidation preference, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution, founders get 2 of 3 board seats. Mega invests $6m at a $12m post-money, 15% pool, 1x participating preference capped at 2.5x, full-ratchet anti-dilution, Mega gets 2 of 3 board seats, CEO shares 25% vested with 36-month monthly repurchase.

parts.prompt: Compare the two term sheets from the founders' perspective: valuation/ownership, anti-dilution, option pool, vesting, board control. Which do you recommend and why?
parts.answer: Mega on valuation/ownership and option pool; Alpha on anti-dilution, vesting and board control. Overall the founders should weigh Mega's higher founder ownership (31.9% vs 26.4%) against Alpha's much stronger governance and downside protection. A common answer is Mega if the founder is growth-confident, Alpha if control and down-round protection dominate.
parts.solution: Alpha: post $9m, price $1, 9m shares; VC 4m (44.4%), angel 0.375m (4.2%), pool 2.25m (25%), founders 26.4%. Mega: post $12m, price $1, 12m shares; VC 6m (50%), angel 0.375m (3.1%), pool 1.80m (15%), founders 31.9%. Mega gives more ownership and a smaller pool; Alpha gives broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution (softer than full ratchet), no forced vesting, and 2 founder board seats vs 1.

parts.prompt: Compute each investor's payoff at exit values of $5m, $10m, $28m and $35m.
parts.answer: Alpha (1x non-participating, 44.4%, LP $4m): $4m, $4.44m, $12.43m, $15.54m. Mega (1x participating, 50%, LP $6m, cap 2.5x = $15m): $5m, $8m, $15m, $17.5m.
parts.solution: Alpha: max(LP, 44.4% × exit) = max(4, 2.22)=4; max(4,4.44)=4.44; max(4,12.43)=12.43; max(4,15.54)=15.54. Mega: LP 6 then 50% of the remainder, capped at 15; if conversion is better, convert. Exit 5: min(5,6)=5. Exit 10: 6+0.5×4=8. Exit 28: 6+0.5×22=17 → cap 15. Exit 35: cap 15 vs conversion 17.5 → 17.5.

parts.prompt: If BD goes with Mega and a Series B is priced at $0.90, how many common shares will Mega's preferred convert to under full ratchet (m)?
parts.solution: Full ratchet cuts the conversion price from $1.00 to $0.90. Mega's 6m preferred shares convert into 6 / 0.90 = 6.667m common shares.

questions.prompt: Magical Genie has two common-equity offers: VW invests $2m at a $5m post-money; XY invests $1m at a $3m pre-money. Founder Ali Baba owns 3m shares. After one year the company is sold for $10m, but it may need a second round: Scenario 1 needs $1m at $2/share (75% probability); Scenario 2 needs $2m at $0.25/share (25%).

parts.prompt: Initial round: compute pre-money, post-money, price per share, investor shares, total shares and founder ownership for each offer.
parts.answer: VW: pre $3m, post $5m, price $1, investor 2m shares, total 5m, founder 60%. XY: pre $3m, post $4m, price $1, investor 1m shares, total 4m, founder 75%.
parts.solution: VW: post = 5, pre = 5 - 2 = 3, price = 3/3 = $1, investor = 2/1 = 2m, total = 5m, founder = 3/5 = 60%. XY: post = 3 + 1 = 4, price = 3/3 = $1, investor = 1/1 = 1m, total = 4m, founder = 3/4 = 75%.

parts.prompt: Second round under each scenario: compute new shares and founder ownership.
parts.answer: Scenario 1: VW unchanged at 60%; XY issues 0.5m at $2, total 4.5m, founder 66.7%. Scenario 2: VW issues 4m at $0.25, total 9m, founder 33.3%; XY issues 8m at $0.25, total 12m, founder 25%.
parts.solution: Scenario 1: VW needs 0; XY raises 1/2 = 0.5m shares → 3/4.5 = 66.7%. Scenario 2: VW raises 1/0.25 = 4m → 3/9 = 33.3%; XY raises 2/0.25 = 8m → 3/12 = 25%.

parts.prompt: With Scenario 1 at 75% probability, compute each offer's expected founder wealth at a $10m exit and recommend one.
parts.solution: Expected ownership: VW = 0.75×0.60 + 0.25×0.3333 = 0.5333; XY = 0.75×0.6667 + 0.25×0.25 = 0.5625. Expected wealth = ownership × $10m: VW $5.333m, XY $5.625m. XY wins by $0.292m, but the difference is small and depends on the probability estimate.
